metadata.title: Multi-scale Neural Networks for Retinal Blood Vessels Segmentation

extraction_notes.note: Network architecture and augmentation are described in prose and figures, not pseudocode; extracted as unmarked algorithms with judgment-based step boundaries.

Per-metric experimental comparisons (individual percentages per dataset), dataset descriptions, the Adam training setup and the robustness discussion were not extracted; only the per-section summary sentences became numerical claims. Result tables in the appendix carry no math.
claim or remark: empirical benchmark statements, kept as numerically supported claims since the abstract announces them as contributions.

metadata.extraction_comment: Applied deep-learning paper with only two displayed equations, both imported (atrous convolution, ACE).

nodes.name: Fully convolutional encoder-decoder segmentation model
nodes.statement: Our model adopts the fully convolutional neural network which is commonly used in most semantic segmentation tasks. It can be briefly divided into two parts - encoder and decoder. The encoder is a convolutional neural network which extracts features from the input image such as the retinal blood vessels image and the decoder will upsample the extracted features to the result image that we desired, such as the vessels segmentation in our task.
nodes.statement_short: Fully convolutional network: encoder extracts features from the retinal image, decoder upsamples them to the vessel segmentation map.

nodes.name: Encoder
nodes.statement: The encoder is a convolutional neural network which extracts features from the input image such as the retinal blood vessels image
nodes.statement_short: Encode: extract features with a CNN.

nodes.name: Decoder
nodes.statement: the decoder will upsample the extracted features to the result image that we desired, such as the vessels segmentation in our task.
nodes.statement_short: Decode: upsample features to the segmentation image.

nodes.name: Convolution-Only Neural Network
nodes.statement:
Therefore we choose to use convolution operation with stride 2 to replace pooling operation so that the information could be preserved as much as possible and the result feature map has the same size as in pooling layer. This architecture is shown in Figure 1 (1).

Another modification in the convolutional layer is that we fuse the features extracted from two adjacent convolutional layers together. So that the low-level information could be passed to the top layers and the model could make sufficient use of the effective low-level features to do semantic segmentation.
nodes.statement_short: Replace pooling by stride-2 convolutions and fuse features of adjacent convolutional layers to pass low-level information upward.

nodes.name: Stride-2 convolution instead of pooling
nodes.statement: Therefore we choose to use convolution operation with stride 2 to replace pooling operation so that the information could be preserved as much as possible and the result feature map has the same size as in pooling layer.
nodes.statement_short: Downsample with stride-2 convolution rather than pooling.

nodes.name: Fuse adjacent-layer features
nodes.statement: Another modification in the convolutional layer is that we fuse the features extracted from two adjacent convolutional layers together. So that the low-level information could be passed to the top layers and the model could make sufficient use of the effective low-level features to do semantic segmentation.
nodes.statement_short: Fuse features of two adjacent convolutional layers.

nodes.name: Atrous convolution
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Atrous Convolution} Atrous convolution is an operation that adds "holes" in normal convolutional operation so that the resolution of features could be controlled by these "holes".

nodes.name: Atrous convolution operation (formula)
nodes.statement_short: Atrous convolution with rate $r$: $y[i]=\sum_k x[i+r k]W[k]$.

nodes.name: Atrous convolution formula
nodes.statement: y [ i ] = \sum _ { k } x [ i + r \cdot k ] W [ k ]

nodes.name: Multi-scale sensitive atrous convolution module
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Multi-scale sensitive features} In order to get multi-scale information, we apply 6 atrous convolutional layers with different rate, 1 max pooling layer and 1 average pooling layer simultaneously on the input image, and then concatenate the extracted feature maps to obtain the effective multi-scale feature map, as shown in Figure 1 (2).
nodes.statement_short: Apply 6 atrous convolutions of different rates plus max and average pooling in parallel, then concatenate into a multi-scale feature map.

nodes.name: Parallel atrous convolutions and poolings
nodes.statement: we apply 6 atrous convolutional layers with different rate, 1 max pooling layer and 1 average pooling layer simultaneously on the input image

nodes.name: Concatenate feature maps
nodes.statement: then concatenate the extracted feature maps to obtain the effective multi-scale feature map, as shown in Figure 1 (2).

nodes.name: Global Contrast Normalization (GCN)
nodes.statement: For the purpose of better response of neural networks, we perform global contrast normalization that every patch of retinal images is standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of its elements.
differentia: every patch of retinal images is standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of its elements

nodes.name: Automatic Color Enhancement (ACE)
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Automatic Color Enhancement (ACE)} Besides GCN, the automatic color enhancement (ACE), which is a smoothed and localized modification method of the normalized histogram equalization, adjusts the contrast of retinal images to achieve the perceptual constancy of color and brightness.
nodes.genus: a smoothed and localized modification method of the normalized histogram equalization
differentia: adjusts the contrast of retinal images to achieve the perceptual constancy of color and brightness

nodes.name: Automatic Color Enhancement (ACE)
nodes.statement_short: ACE: split RGB channels and scale to [0,1], compute local contrast $R(x)$ via slope-function differences, stretch to [0,1], then optimize.

nodes.name: Separate channels and scale
nodes.statement: First, we separate the RGB channels of one retinal image $I(x)$  with domain $\Omega$  and scale intensity values to $[0, 1]$.

nodes.name: Compute local contrast R(x)
nodes.statement_short: Compute $R(x)$ as distance-weighted sum of slope-function intensity differences.

nodes.name: ACE local contrast R(x)
nodes.statement: R(x) = \sum_{y \in \Omega /\ x}\frac{s_a(I(x) - I(y))}{\left \| x-y \right \|} \ \ \ x \in \Omega

nodes.name: Stretch R to [0,1]
nodes.statement: For the purpose of the global white balance, we extend $R(x)$ to $[0, 1]$.

nodes.name: Solve optimization problem
nodes.statement: Finally, we solve the optimization problem.

nodes.name: ACE complexity
nodes.statement: For one retinal image, the complexity of the ACE is $O(N^4)$ and it is too slow to handle all retinal images.
conclusions: the complexity of the ACE is $O(N^4)$

nodes.name: Improved ACE algorithm (Getreuer)
nodes.statement: Therefore, we use an improved ACE algorithm proposed by Pascal Getreuer [13]. The new algorithm adopts two approximate methods that they both significantly improve the speed of ACE. One uses polynomial function to approximate the slope function to reduce the calculation and the other uses different degrees of interpolation.
nodes.statement_short: Fast ACE approximation: polynomial approximation of the slope function plus interpolation over levels.

nodes.name: Polynomial slope approximation
nodes.statement: One uses polynomial function to approximate the slope function to reduce the calculation

nodes.name: Interpolation
nodes.statement: the other uses different degrees of interpolation.

nodes.name: Patch augmentation
nodes.statement: First, the decision of random cropping on the class of a particular 64 $\times$ 64 pixel is based on a   patch centered at that pixel of retinal images. For example, we can get a 64 $\times$ 64 $\times$ 3 vector for each patch of retinal images. It should be pointed out that we extract patches after preprocess methods because of the consideration of training and test speed. To further explore augmentations, each patch of retinal images is composed of limited four randomized actions as follows: a) Flipping horizontally or vertically; b) Gamma correction of Saturation and Value (of the HSV colorspace) by raising pixels to a power in [0.25, 4]; c) Rotation by an angle in [-90, 90]; d) Scaling by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3.
nodes.statement_short: Crop 64x64 patches, then randomly flip, gamma-correct S/V, rotate and scale each patch.

nodes.name: Random 64x64 patch cropping
nodes.statement: First, the decision of random cropping on the class of a particular 64 $\times$ 64 pixel is based on a   patch centered at that pixel of retinal images.

nodes.name: Four randomized actions
nodes.statement: To further explore augmentations, each patch of retinal images is composed of limited four randomized actions as follows: a) Flipping horizontally or vertically; b) Gamma correction of Saturation and Value (of the HSV colorspace) by raising pixels to a power in [0.25, 4]; c) Rotation by an angle in [-90, 90]; d) Scaling by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3.
nodes.statement_short: Apply up to four random transformations per patch.

nodes.name: Flip
nodes.statement: a) Flipping horizontally or vertically

nodes.name: Gamma correction
nodes.statement: b) Gamma correction of Saturation and Value (of the HSV colorspace) by raising pixels to a power in [0.25, 4]

nodes.name: Rotate
nodes.statement: c) Rotation by an angle in [-90, 90]

nodes.name: Scale
nodes.statement: d) Scaling by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3.

nodes.name: Structure prediction variants sp-1, sp-32, sp-64
nodes.statement: The windows of sp-1, sp-32 and sp-64 are the whole image, 32 $\times$ 32 and 64 $\times$ 64 respectively. The stride of sp-1, sp-32 and sp-64 are 1, 3 and 3 respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Sliding-window test-time predictions: whole image stride 1, 32x32 stride 3, 64x64 stride 3.

nodes.name: Evaluation metrics (AUC, Acc, Sens, Spec, test speed)
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Evaluation metrics} The evaluation metrics of our experiment is divided into two parts, one is in terms of area under ROC curve AUC, accuracy Acc, sensitivity Sens, specificity Spec and the other is the test speed that process one image (average time).

nodes.name: DRIVE performance improvement
nodes.statement: In summary, our model leads the AUC, accuracy and specificity of baseline by at least 0.6200\%, 0.7300\% and 1.200\% respectively.
conclusions: our model leads the AUC, accuracy and specificity of baseline by at least 0.6200\%, 0.7300\% and 1.200\% respectively

nodes.name: STARE performance improvement
nodes.statement: In summary, our method also achieves better performance than several existing method for the same criteria although the improvement of the STARE dataset is lower than that on the DRIVE dataset and this may be due to the high AUC that exceeds 99\%.
conclusions: our method also achieves better performance than several existing method for the same criteria

nodes.name: CHASE performance improvement
nodes.statement: In summary, our method also achieves better performance than several existing method in CHASE dataset.
conclusions: our method also achieves better performance than several existing method in CHASE dataset

nodes.name: Test speed of SP-1
nodes.statement: In summary, the SP-1 achieves the test time of 3s, which is 7s faster than the state-of-the-art unsupervised method [6], and 87s faster than the state-of-the-art supervised method [12].
conclusions: the SP-1 achieves the test time of 3s
